note: Rabbi Meir sent Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar to bring wine from the Samaritans' area. An old man met him and quoted a verse from Proverbs at him: 'And put a knife to your throat, if you are a man given to appetite.' Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar reported this to Rabbi Meir, who issued a decree against them.
why: The Gemara asks why the Sages forbade eating meat slaughtered by Samaritans, and answers with this incident. It then explains that some Samaritans on Mount Gerizim worshipped an image of a dove, and Rabbi Meir took that minority into account.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: Sends his student for wine and then decrees against the Samaritans.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
people.about: Sent by Rabbi Meir to bring wine.

people.name: a certain elder
people.about: Warns Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar with a verse.

terms.meaning: A people living in the Land of Israel whose observance the Sages here judged unreliable.
A rule the Sages issue on their own authority to protect against a problem.

note: Rabbi Abbahu sent Rabbi Yitzḥak ben Yosef to bring wine from the Samaritans' area. An old man met him and told him that the people there were not keepers of the Torah. Rabbi Yitzḥak told Rabbi Abbahu, Rabbi Abbahu told Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi, and they did not leave the spot until they had declared the Samaritans full-fledged gentiles.
why: It parallels the earlier incident that led Rabbi Meir to decree against the Samaritans. The Gemara then asks what this later decree added, and answers that the earlier one was not accepted by the people, while this one was.

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: Sends Rabbi Yitzḥak ben Yosef for wine and passes on the report.

people.name: Rabbi Yitzḥak ben Yosef
people.about: Sent to bring wine from the Samaritans.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: With Rabbi Asi, declares the Samaritans full-fledged gentiles.

people.name: Rabbi Asi
people.about: With Rabbi Ami, declares the Samaritans full-fledged gentiles.

terms.meaning: Treated in Jewish law as non-Jews; the Gemara goes on to apply this to the Shabbat rules for shared courtyards.
A people living in the Land of Israel whose observance the Sages doubted.

note: Rabbi Zeira and Rav Asi stopped at the inn of Ya'ei and were served eggs shriveled in wine. Rabbi Zeira did not eat; Rav Asi did. Rabbi Zeira asked whether he was not worried that the dish contained demai wine, and Rav Asi said it had not crossed his mind. Rabbi Zeira reasoned that God does not let even the animals of the righteous cause a mishap, so surely Rav Asi would not have been led to eat forbidden food. He went out, looked into it, and found a teaching showing that no mishap had happened.
why: The Gemara has used the principle that God keeps the righteous from mishaps to argue that Rabbi Yoḥanan and Rabbi Asi ate Samaritan meat knowingly. It returns to that principle here, and then tests whether the Sages ever forbade mixtures containing demai.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: Refuses the eggs, then reasons that Rav Asi could not have eaten forbidden food.

people.name: Rav Asi
people.about: Eats the eggs without thinking about the wine.

terms.meaning: Produce bought from someone not trusted to have separated the required tithes, which must be tithed again in case it was not.
Portions of produce that must be set aside for priests, Levites and others before the rest may be eaten.

note: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Zeruz, son of Rabbi Meir's father-in-law, testified before Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi that Rabbi Meir had eaten a vegetable leaf in Beit She'an without tithing it, and Rabbi permitted all the produce of Beit She'an on that basis. His brothers and his father's household united against him: would he permit what his fathers and their fathers had treated as forbidden? He answered from the verse about Hezekiah smashing the copper serpent Moses had made: could the righteous kings Asa and Jehoshaphat, who destroyed all idol worship, have left it standing? Rather, Hezekiah's ancestors had left him room to distinguish himself, and his own ancestors had left room for him too.
why: The Gemara is collecting cases for the principle that the righteous do not stumble into eating forbidden food, and treats Rabbi Meir's eating as deliberate. From Rabbi's reply it learns that a scholar who states a new ruling is not to be dismissed.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Zeruz
people.about: Son of Rabbi Meir's father-in-law; testifies about what Rabbi Meir ate.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: Ate an untithed vegetable leaf in Beit She'an.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called simply 'Rabbi'; permits Beit She'an's produce and defends the ruling to his family.

terms.meaning: Portions of produce grown in the Land of Israel that must be given to priests and Levites; until they are separated the produce may not be eaten.
A town whose produce, according to this ruling, did not need tithing; the text explains Rabbi Meir held it was not sanctified as part of the Land of Israel.
The bronze snake Moses made in the wilderness, which the people later burned incense to, until King Hezekiah broke it.

note: Rabbi Pineḥas ben Ya'ir was on his way to redeem captives when he reached the Ginai River and told it to part so he could cross. The river answered that both of them were doing their Maker's will, but his success was uncertain while the river's was certain. He threatened to decree that water would never flow in it again, and it parted. He then had it part for a man carrying wheat for Passover matza, who was doing a mitzva, and for an Arab traveling with them, so that he would not say this is how a companion is treated. Each time the river parted.
why: Rabbi Zeira argued that since God does not let even the animals of the righteous cause a mishap, the righteous themselves surely do not stumble. The Gemara asks what animals he meant, and begins this story of Rabbi Pineḥas ben Ya'ir, whose donkey is the answer.

people.name: Rabbi Pineḥas ben Ya'ir
people.about: A Sage traveling to redeem captives, who commands a river to part.

people.name: the Ginai River
people.about: The river that argues with him and then parts.

people.name: a certain man
people.about: Carrying wheat for Passover matza.

people.name: a certain Arab
people.about: Traveling with them.

terms.meaning: Paying ransom to free people held captive, counted among the greatest of good deeds.
A commandment, or a good deed done in fulfillment of one.
Unleavened bread eaten on Passover.

note: After crossing the river, Rabbi Pineḥas ben Ya'ir stopped at an inn, and his hosts put barley before his donkey, but it would not eat. They sifted the barley, then picked it clean by hand, and still it refused. He suggested that perhaps the barley was not tithed; they tithed it, and the donkey ate. He said: 'This poor animal is going to do the will of its Maker, and you feed it untithed produce?'
why: This is the donkey Rabbi Zeira meant when he said God does not let the animals of the righteous cause a mishap. The Gemara then asks why the barley needed tithing, since grain bought for animals is exempt, and answers with a distinction from Rabbi Yoḥanan.

people.name: Rabbi Pineḥas ben Ya'ir
people.about: A Sage on a journey to redeem captives, whose donkey refuses untithed barley.

terms.meaning: Produce from which the portions owed to priests and Levites have not been set aside; it may not be eaten.

note: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi went out to meet Rabbi Pineḥas ben Ya'ir and invited him to dine; he accepted, and Rabbi's face beamed. He explained that he usually declined because some hosts want to but cannot afford it and some can but do not want to, while Rabbi both could and wanted to; but he was hurrying to a mitzva and would come back. On his return he passed a gate where white mules stood and said: 'The Angel of Death is in this man's house, and I will eat with him?' Rabbi offered to sell the mules, abandon them, cut their hooves or kill them, and each time he named a prohibition. As Rabbi kept pleading, a mountain rose between them. Rabbi wept, saying the righteous are greater after death than in life.
why: It continues the Gemara's account of Rabbi Pineḥas ben Ya'ir's journey, begun to explain Rabbi Zeira's saying about the animals of the righteous. The Elisha verse at its end is then debated by Rav Pappa and Abaye.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called 'Rabbi'; invites Rabbi Pineḥas ben Ya'ir to dine.

people.name: Rabbi Pineḥas ben Ya'ir
people.about: A Sage who rarely accepted invitations; he accepts, then refuses because of the mules.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥama bar Ḥanina
people.about: Quoted by the Gemara: the righteous are greater after death, proved from Elisha's bones.

terms.meaning: The text treats them as deadly animals, likened to the Angel of Death.
A Torah prohibition, here applied to selling a dangerous animal to someone else.
The duty not to cause animals needless pain.
The prohibition on wasting or destroying things of value.

note: A certain woman kept trying to take dust from under Rabbi Ḥanina's feet to use in sorcery against him. He told her: 'Take it. It will not work for you, for it is written: There is none else beside Him.' The Gemara asks how this fits Rabbi Yoḥanan's saying that sorcery works against the heavenly entourage, and answers that Rabbi Ḥanina was different because his merit was great.
why: The Gemara is gathering sayings of Rabbi Ḥanina after quoting his warning about white mules. This episode illustrates his teaching that the verse 'There is none else beside Him' covers even sorcery.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥanina
people.about: The Sage whom the woman tries to bewitch.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: Quoted as saying sorcery works against the heavenly powers.

terms.meaning: Magic used to harm someone. Rabbi Yoḥanan reads its Hebrew name, keshafim, as saying it goes against the heavenly entourage.
The angels and powers on high that carry out God's will.

note: Ravina and Rav Aḥa, son of Rava, were sitting before Rav Ashi when a knife was brought to him to be checked. He told Rav Aḥa to check it, and Rav Aḥa examined it on the fingernail, on the flesh and on all three sides. Rav Ashi said to him, 'Well done', and added that Rav Kahana had said the same.
why: The Gemara has been listing ways to check a slaughtering knife, and gave conflicting reports of whether Rav Ashi required checking the three sides. Here he approves that full check; Rav Yeimar then argues the sides need no checking.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: Sitting before Rav Ashi.

people.name: Rav Aḥa, son of Rava
people.about: Checks the knife at Rav Ashi's request.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: The teacher who is brought the knife and approves the check.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: Cited by Rav Ashi as teaching the same method.

terms.meaning: Checking a slaughtering knife for notches, which would tear rather than cut and make the slaughter invalid.
The cutting edge and the two flat faces of the blade.

note: A slaughterer failed to show his knife to Rava bar Hinnana for inspection. Rava bar Hinnana ostracized him, removed him from his post and proclaimed his meat tereifa, forbidden. When Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi visited, Rava bar Hinnana asked them to look into the man's case, since small children depended on him. Rav Ashi checked the knife, found it intact and declared the meat fit. Mar Zutra asked whether he should not worry about the elder's honor; Rav Ashi answered that they were acting as the elder's own agents, since he had asked them to examine the matter.
why: Rav Huna said a slaughterer who does not show his knife to a scholar is ostracized, and Rava said he is removed and his meat declared tereifa; the Gemara reconciled them by whether the knife turns out intact. Here a knife found intact leads to the meat being permitted.

people.name: Rava bar Hinnana
people.about: The Sage who punished the slaughterer and then asked visitors to review the case.

people.name: Mar Zutra
people.about: A visiting Sage who worries about Rava bar Hinnana's honor.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: A visiting Sage who examines the knife and permits the meat.

terms.meaning: A formal ban by a rabbinic court that cuts a person off from the community until he mends his ways.
An animal with a fatal defect or injury. Even if slaughtered properly, its meat may not be eaten.

note: When Rabbi Zeira moved from Babylonia to the Land of Israel, he ate meat from an animal whose slaughter Rav and Shmuel, the authorities of Babylonia, were reported to rule invalid. The local scholars asked whether he was not from the place of Rav and Shmuel. He replied that the report came from Yosef bar Hiyya (Rav Yosef), who learns from everyone. Rav Yosef heard and was angry: he learned from Rav Yehuda, who was so careful that he even passed on his doubts about which Sage had said something.
why: The Gemara has just set out where Rav and Shmuel agree and disagree with Rabbi Yosei on valid slaughter. Afterwards it asks why Rabbi Zeira did not keep the stricter custom of the place he came from, and Abaye and Rav Ashi explain why.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: A Sage who moved from Babylonia to the Land of Israel and ate meat Babylonian authorities forbade.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Also called Yosef bar Hiyya; the Sage who reported Rav and Shmuel's ruling and was angered by Rabbi Zeira's remark.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Rav Yosef's teacher, careful to report even his doubts about who said what.

people.name: Rav and Shmuel
people.about: The leading Babylonian authorities whose ruling is in question.

terms.meaning: A firstborn male animal was holy and given to a priest; if it had a blemish it could be slaughtered and eaten, but only after a qualified Sage ruled on the blemish.

note: A Roman official put a question to Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai: one verse in Genesis says birds came from the water, another says God formed them from the ground. Rabban Yohanan answered that they were created from mud, a mix of both. Seeing his students exchange looks, he asked whether it bothered them that he had pushed off his opponent with a flimsy answer. He then told them that birds were really created from water, and are mentioned with the ground only because they were brought to Adam to be named.
why: The Gemara has just quoted a teaching that birds, made from mud, need only one of the two signs cut in slaughter, between land animals and fish. This exchange turns on the same question of what birds were made from.

people.name: Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai
people.about: The Sage who answers the official one way and his students another.

people.name: the official
people.about: A Roman government official who asks about two verses that seem to contradict each other.

people.name: Adam
people.about: The first man, to whom God brought the birds to be named.

note: Rava would check an arrow for Rabbi Yona bar Tahlifa to make sure it had no nicks, and Rabbi Yona shot a bird in flight with it, cutting its neck as a slaughter. The Gemara raises doubts: perhaps the arrow cut the wrong way, from inside the neck? No, it answers: the feathers at the front of the neck were torn, showing the cut came from the front. And how could the blood be covered with earth below and above, as the law requires? The Gemara answers that he set aside the earth of the whole valley beforehand to serve as the earth beneath.
why: The Gemara has just learned from a verse about a drawn arrow that slaughter means drawing the blade across the neck, not pressing or striking. This case shows slaughter done with an actual arrow.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who examined the arrow.

people.name: Rabbi Yona bar Tahlifa
people.about: The man who shot and slaughtered the flying bird.

terms.meaning: A commandment that when a wild animal or bird is slaughtered, its blood is covered with earth. The Sages read the verse to require earth both under and over the blood.
The windpipe and gullet, which must be cut for a slaughter to be valid.

note: A healthy man said, "Write a bill of divorce for my wife." He then went up to the roof, fell and died. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel ruled that if he fell on purpose, the bill of divorce is valid; if the wind pushed him, it is not.
why: The Gemara is looking for the source of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's view that a person's final actions reveal what he meant at the start; it considers this ruling, then argues it may not prove the point, since here the man's words already showed his intent.

people.name: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
people.about: The Sage who rules on whether the dead man's divorce order holds.

terms.meaning: In Hebrew a get: the document a husband must give his wife to end a marriage. Here the question is whether others may write and deliver it on his instructions.

note: Some Arabs came to Tzikuneya and gave rams to Jewish slaughterers, saying: the blood and the fat are for us, the hide and meat for you. Rav Tuvi bar Rav Mattana sent the question to Rav Yosef: what is the law in such a case? Rav Yosef sent back that Rav Yehuda had said in Shmuel's name that the law follows Rabbi Yosei.
why: The mishna records a dispute over a Jew slaughtering for a gentile who means it for idol worship; Rabbi Yosei says only the slaughterer's intent matters, and Shmuel ruled like him. This case puts that ruling into practice.

people.name: Rav Tuvi bar Rav Mattana
people.about: The Sage who sent the question about the rams.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: The Sage who answered, citing Rav Yehuda in Shmuel's name.

note: An animal was brought to Rabba because it might have been clawed by a predator. Rabba began checking its gullet from the outside. Abaye said to him: wasn't it you, Master, who said the gullet can be checked only from the inside? Rabba turned it over, checked inside, found two drops of blood and ruled it tereifa. The Gemara adds that Rabba had only wanted to sharpen Abaye.
why: Rabba had taught that the gullet must be checked from the inside, since its outer lining is red anyway, and the Gemara said this matters when an animal may have been clawed. Here is that very case.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: The Sage who checks the animal and rules on it.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Rabba's student, who reminds him of his own teaching.

terms.meaning: An animal with a fatal defect or injury. Even if slaughtered properly, its meat may not be eaten.
The food pipe running from the throat to the stomach. A hole in it makes the animal forbidden.

note: A bull belonging to the sons of Rav Ukva was slaughtered with a cut that began at the entrance of the gullet and finished in the gullet itself. Rava declared it tereifa, saying he was applying both Rav's stringency and Shmuel's: with Shmuel, the entrance is not a valid place to slaughter, so the first cut counts as damage; with Rav, damage of any size there makes the animal forbidden. The case reached Rabbi Abba, who said the bull was permitted by both Rav and Shmuel, and told them to go tell Rava to pay the owner the value of the bull.
why: Rav and Shmuel disagree on the entrance of the gullet: Rav says any hole there is fatal because it counts as part of the gullet; Shmuel says only a large one is, because it is not. Afterwards the Gemara cites a teaching that taking two schools' stringencies together is foolish.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Also called the son of Rav Yosef bar Hama; he declares the bull forbidden.

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: The Sage who rules the bull permitted and says Rava must pay.

people.name: Rav and Shmuel
people.about: Two Sages whose opposing rulings Rava combines.

terms.meaning: An animal with a fatal defect or injury. Even if slaughtered properly, its meat may not be eaten.
The point where the throat opens into the food pipe. Sages disagree whether it counts as part of the gullet.

note: Rav Tavut said Rava had in fact followed Rav alone. When Rami bar Yehezkel came, he said: do not listen to the rules my brother Rav Yehuda taught in Rav's name. Rav really said that the Sages set a measure for the part of the gullet where slaughter is valid, which shows the entrance is not a valid place to slaughter, and yet he said a hole of any size there is fatal.
why: The Gemara has just called Rava's ruling on the bull difficult, since he seemed to combine two opposite stringencies. Rav Tavut defends him: Rav himself held both positions, so Rava followed one Sage.

people.name: Rav Tavut
people.about: The Sage who defends Rava's ruling.

people.name: Rami bar Yehezkel
people.about: Brother of Rav Yehuda; he corrected the rules Rav Yehuda reported in Rav's name.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Rami bar Yehezkel's brother, who taught rules in Rav's name.

terms.meaning: The point where the throat opens into the food pipe. Sages disagree whether it counts as part of the gullet.

flag: Mostly a statement of who said what in Rav's name; the only event is Rami bar Yehezkel's arrival and remark.

note: An animal with a cut windpipe was brought to Rav, who sat checking whether most of the windpipe's thickness was cut. Rav Kahana and Rav Asi said to him: you taught us, our teacher, that it is measured by most of the inner space. Rav sent it to Rabba bar bar Hana, who checked it by the inner space, ruled it kosher, and bought meat from it for thirteen plain istera coins.
why: The Gemara has just reported two versions of Rav's view on how much of a windpipe must be cut to make an animal forbidden: most of its thickness, or most of its inner space. Afterwards it asks how Rabba bar bar Hana could permit it after Rav, and eat from it.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The teacher who began checking the animal and then sent it on.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: Rav's student, who reminds him of his teaching.

people.name: Rav Asi
people.about: Rav's student, who joins in reminding him.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Hana
people.about: The Sage who rules the animal kosher and buys its meat.

terms.meaning: A small coin.

note: A lung with an extra lobe was brought to Mareimar while Rav Aha sat at the door. Rav Aha asked the owner what Mareimar had said, and he answered that it was ruled kosher. Rav Aha told him to go back and bring it before Mareimar again. Mareimar said to him: go tell whoever is sitting at the door that the law does not follow Rava in the case of an extra lobe.
why: Rava has just taught that a lung with a missing, extra or misplaced lobe makes the animal tereifa, forbidden. Mareimar's ruling rejects that rule for an extra lobe, and the Gemara then limits where the lobe may be.

people.name: Mareimar
people.about: The Sage who ruled the lung kosher.

people.name: Rav Aha
people.about: A Sage sitting at Mareimar's door who questioned the ruling.

terms.meaning: One of the sections of the lung. Normally an animal has three on one side and two on the other.

note: Rabbi Natan told how he once traveled to the cities overseas. A woman came to him whose first son had died after circumcision, and her second as well; she brought her third son to him. He saw the baby was red and told her: my daughter, wait until his blood is absorbed. She waited, then circumcised him, and he lived. People called the boy Natan the Babylonian, after him.
why: The Gemara rules that a red or green lung does not make an animal forbidden, and cites Rabbi Natan's babies who recovered from those colors as the proof that such a condition can heal.

people.name: Rabbi Natan
people.about: The Sage who advised the mother to wait before circumcising.

people.name: the woman
people.about: A mother who had lost two sons after circumcision.

note: Rabbi Natan told how he went another time to Cappadocia. A woman came whose first and second sons had died after circumcision, and she brought her third. He saw the baby was green and had no blood for circumcision in him. He told her: my daughter, wait until his blood comes into him. She waited, then circumcised him, and he lived. People called the boy Natan the Babylonian, after him.
why: The Gemara rules that a green lung does not make an animal forbidden, and cites this baby who recovered from a green color as proof that such a condition can heal.

people.name: Rabbi Natan
people.about: The Sage who advised the mother to wait before circumcising.

people.name: the woman
people.about: A mother in Cappadocia who had lost two sons after circumcision.

note: Rabbi Hananya fell sick, and Rabbi Natan and all the great scholars of the generation came to visit him. They brought before him a lung that could be poured out like water from a jug, and he ruled the animal kosher.
why: Rabbi Yohanan had ruled that a liquefied lung is kosher, because damage inside an organ does not count; Rabbi Abba challenged this from the mishna. This case supports the ruling, and Rava then limits it to where the bronchi remain.

people.name: Rabbi Hananya
people.about: The sick Sage who rules the lung kosher.

people.name: Rabbi Natan
people.about: One of the scholars who came to visit him.

note: Worms were found in an animal's liver. The people of Asia went up to the Sanhedrin in Yavne about it on three festivals, and on the third they permitted it to them.
why: The Gemara is listing defects that do not make an animal forbidden, after a liquefied or wasted lung; this case shows that a worm-infested liver is also allowed.

terms.meaning: The high court of the Sages. After the Temple's destruction it sat in Yavne.
The three pilgrimage festivals, when people traveled to the center of Jewish life; here, three trips to put the question.

note: Rabbi Yitzhak bar Yosef was walking behind Rabbi Yirmeya in the butchers' market and saw lungs covered in cysts. Hoping to get a ruling, he asked whether the Master wanted some meat. Rabbi Yirmeya said he had no money; Rabbi Yitzhak offered to buy on credit. Rabbi Yirmeya then said: when people came to Rabbi Yohanan with such lungs, he sent them to Rabbi Yehuda son of Rabbi Shimon, who permitted them in his father's name, but Rabbi Yohanan himself did not hold so. Rava adds that when they walked behind Rav Nahman in the market and he saw lungs covered in large cysts, he said nothing to the butchers.
why: Shmuel has just ruled that a lung with cysts is kosher. These scenes show what Sages actually did in the market when they saw such lungs.

people.name: Rabbi Yitzhak bar Yosef
people.about: A Sage who tries to draw a ruling out of Rabbi Yirmeya.

people.name: Rabbi Yirmeya
people.about: The Sage who avoids ruling, then explains Rabbi Yohanan's practice.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: A Sage who sent such questions to another and did not himself permit.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda son of Rabbi Shimon
people.about: A Sage who permitted such lungs in the name of Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: A Sage who saw such lungs in the market and said nothing.

terms.meaning: Swellings on the lung filled with fluid or pus. The question is whether they mean the animal is forbidden.

flag: Combines two separate anecdotes: Rabbi Yirmeya in the butchers' market, and Rava's report about Rav Nahman.

note: A needle was found in a cut piece of lung and brought to Rabbi Ami, who thought to rule it kosher. Rabbi Yirmeya (some say Rabbi Zerika) objected from the mishna: a lung that is missing something is fatal, which must mean a loss inside the lung counts. They sent it to Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha, who also thought to permit it, and the same objection was raised. They sent it back to Rabbi Ami, who ruled it tereifa. Asked why, when the Rabbis permit such a case, he said: they knew their reason, having seen the whole lung; we see only a piece, and perhaps the whole lung would have shown a hole.
why: The Gemara has just reported a dispute over a needle found in a lung, and explained it as a question of whether the needle came in by the airway or pierced through. This case shows why Rabbi Ami would not permit when only part of the lung was there.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: The Sage who first leaned toward permitting, then forbade.

people.name: Rabbi Yirmeya
people.about: The Sage who raised the objection; some say it was Rabbi Zerika.

people.name: Rabbi Zerika
people.about: Named by some as the one who raised the objection.

people.name: Rabbi Yitzhak Nappaha
people.about: A second Sage to whom the lung was sent, who also leaned toward permitting.

terms.meaning: An animal with a fatal defect or injury. Even if slaughtered properly, its meat may not be eaten.
The early collection of rabbinic law that the Gemara discusses and explains.

note: A needle was found in the large duct of an animal's liver. Huna Mar son of Rav Idi ruled it tereifa; Rav Adda bar Minyumi ruled it kosher. They came and asked Ravina, who said: take the robe of those who ruled it tereifa, that is, make them pay the owner for the meat he wrongly threw away.
why: The Gemara has just discussed needles found inside organs, and why some can be assumed to have entered without piercing. Ravina's ruling treats a needle in the liver duct the same way.

people.name: Huna Mar son of Rav Idi
people.about: The Sage who ruled the animal forbidden.

people.name: Rav Adda bar Minyumi
people.about: The Sage who ruled it kosher.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: The Sage who decided that those who forbade it must pay.

terms.meaning: An animal with a fatal defect or injury. Even if slaughtered properly, its meat may not be eaten.

note: Rabbi Hanina's attendant was standing before him, and Rabbi Hanina told him to take off a handful of the fat and give him the rest to eat. Seeing the attendant hesitate, Rabbi Hanina said: you are a Babylonian. Cut it all off and throw it away.
why: The Gemara has explained that Sages of the Land of Israel permitted part of a certain fat on the stomach once a handful was removed, while Babylonians forbade all of it; this scene shows the two customs side by side.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina
people.about: A Sage of the Land of Israel who eats the fat once a handful is removed.

people.name: the attendant
people.about: Rabbi Hanina's servant, a Babylonian who hesitates to handle the fat.

terms.meaning: Removing a handful of the upper fat, which counts as the forbidden fat; by the custom of the Land of Israel, the rest could then be eaten.

note: Some perforated intestines were brought before Rava. He made fresh holes to compare with the old ones, but they did not look alike. His son Rav Mesharshiyya came, rubbed the new holes, and then they looked alike. Rava asked him how he knew to do that. He answered: how many hands handled these before they came to you, Master? Rava said: my son is as wise in matters of tereifot as Rabbi Yohanan.
why: Rav Shimi bar Hiyya has just taught that one may compare holes in the intestines, making a new hole to see whether an old one happened after slaughter. This case shows how to do the comparison fairly.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage before whom the intestines were brought.

people.name: Rav Mesharshiyya
people.about: Rava's son, who rubbed the new holes to make the comparison fair.

terms.meaning: Plural of tereifa: animals with fatal defects whose meat may not be eaten, and the laws about them.
Making a new cut next to an old hole: if they look alike, the old hole happened after slaughter and the animal is kosher.

note: Rav Safra told Abaye about a scholar from the Land of Israel, Rav Avira, who reported that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi had declared an animal a tereifa because of a needle found sticking out of only one side of its stomach wall. Abaye sent for him; Rav Avira did not come, so Abaye went to him. Rav Avira was standing on a roof and would not come down, so Abaye climbed up and asked what had actually happened. Rav Avira said he had been present: Rabbi turned the stomach wall over, found a drop of blood on the outside, and ruled it a tereifa, asking where the blood could come from if there was no wound there. Abaye retorted that he had been troubled for nothing, since this is simply the mishna's rule about a stomach perforated to the outside.
why: The Gemara has been discussing needles found in an animal's stomach and how a drop of blood shows a wound came before slaughter. Rav Avira's report seemed to clash with the rule that a needle makes an animal a tereifa only if it pierces right through.

people.name: Rav Safra
people.about: The Sage who tells Abaye about the visiting scholar's report.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: The Sage who goes to great lengths to question Rav Avira, then finds the case adds nothing new.

people.name: Rav Avira
people.about: A Torah scholar from the Land of Israel who says he witnessed the ruling; he refuses to come down from the roof.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called 'Rabbi' and 'the Great Rabbi'; the teacher who inspected the animal and ruled on it.

people.name: Rav Huna of Tzippori
people.about: One of two scholars Rav Avira says were sitting before Rabbi when the case came up.

terms.meaning: An animal with a fatal injury or defect. Its meat is forbidden to eat even if it was slaughtered properly.
One of the chambers of a cow's or sheep's stomach; its wall is thick, so a needle can lodge inside it.
The early collection of Jewish law on which the Gemara comments. Here it lists stomach perforations that make an animal a tereifa.
Rav Avira's description of his job in the study hall; it explains why he was standing near Rabbi and saw the case himself.

note: A young goat belonging to Ravina saw barley groats through an open skylight, jumped through it and fell from the roof to the ground. The case came before Rav Ashi. Ravina asked him why Rav Huna rules that an animal left on a roof and found below need not be checked for shattered limbs: is it because animals usually have something to grab on the way down, which this goat did not, or because an animal judges for itself whether it can make the jump, which this goat also did? Rav Ashi answered that it is because the animal judges itself, and this goat did so too.
why: The mishna says an animal that fell from a roof is a tereifa, and Rav Huna has just limited that to falls nobody saw happen. Ravina's goat tests the reason behind Rav Huna's leniency.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: Owner of the young goat; he puts the question to Rav Ashi.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: The Sage the case came before; he rules that the goat need not be suspected of injury.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: The Sage whose earlier ruling about animals found below a roof Ravina asks about.

terms.meaning: Internal crushing injuries from a fall. If suspected, the animal may be a tereifa, an animal with a fatal defect whose meat is forbidden.

note: A bull fell in the slaughterhouse, and its bellowing from the blow could be heard. Even so, Rav Yitzḥak bar Shmuel bar Marta went in and took some of the very best cuts of its meat. The Sages asked him how he knew this was allowed. He answered with a teaching of Rav: when a bull falls, it digs in its hooves until it reaches the ground.
why: Rav Naḥman has just ruled that an animal thrown down in the slaughterhouse is not suspected of shattered limbs. This incident shows the ruling applied even to a fall loud enough to hear.

people.name: Rav Yitzḥak bar Shmuel bar Marta
people.about: The Sage who took the best meat of the fallen bull without worry and explained why.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage whose teaching about how a bull falls Rav Yitzḥak quotes.

terms.meaning: An animal with a fatal injury or defect, such as crushed internal organs from a bad fall. Its meat is forbidden even if properly slaughtered.

note: In the house of Rav Kahana, a cat chased a hen into a small room. The door shut in the cat's face, and the cat struck the door with its paws in anger. Afterward five drops of blood, which the Gemara understands as the cat's venom, were found on the door.
why: The Gemara is discussing whether a cat's claw is venomous enough to make a small animal a tereifa only when bystanders try to save the prey. The hen incident is raised as a challenge, since the cat produced venom with no one there to save the hen.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: The Sage in whose house the hen was kept.

terms.meaning: An animal with a fatal injury or defect; its meat is forbidden even if properly slaughtered. A predator's venomous clawing can make an animal one.

note: In the house of Rav Kahana, a cat chased a hen into a small room. The door shut in the cat's face, and the cat struck the door with its paws in anger. Afterward five drops of blood, which the Gemara understands as the cat's venom, were found on the door. The Gemara answers that for a cat, saving itself counts the same as when others try to save its prey.
why: In the second version of the debate, the view that a cat's claw is venomous only when someone is there to save the prey is challenged by this incident. The Gemara's answer keeps that view standing.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: The Sage in whose house the hen was kept.

terms.meaning: Bystanders trying to rescue an animal from a predator. One view holds that this angers the predator so that its claws become venomous.

note: A basket of birds came before Rav. A hawk had got in among them, and it was uncertain whether it had clawed them. Rav sent the birds to Shmuel, and Shmuel strangled them and threw them into the river.
why: Rav and Shmuel disagree on whether a possible clawing must be treated as real. The Gemara suggests this case shows Rav retracted and came round to Shmuel; the discussion then rejects that, saying Rav sent the birds because it was Shmuel's town.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage the birds were first brought to; he passed them on to Shmuel.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The Sage who strangled the birds and threw them in the river.

terms.meaning: Attacked by a predator's claws. A bird clawed by a hawk is treated as a tereifa, an animal with a fatal injury whose meat is forbidden.

note: Rabba bar bar Ḥana was walking in the desert and found some rams whose lungs were shriveled. He came and asked in the study hall what to do. The Sages told him how to test such lungs: in summer, put them in white vessels of cold water for twenty-four hours, and in winter in dark vessels of tepid water. If the lungs return to looking healthy, the shriveling was from Heaven and the animals are kosher; if not, they are tereifa. The text does not say what he found when he tested them.
why: The mishna rules that a lung shriveled by the hand of Heaven is kosher, while a baraita says one shriveled by a person's doing is a tereifa. This story gives the practical test for telling the two apart.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Ḥana
people.about: The Sage who found the rams in the desert and brought the question to the study hall.

terms.meaning: From natural causes rather than from something a person did; for example, a lung shriveled by fright at thunder.
An animal with a fatal defect; its meat is forbidden even if it was slaughtered properly.

note: A hen in the house of Rav Ḥana had a head injury, and he sent it to Rav Mattana. Rav Mattana found that the skull bone was broken but the membrane of the brain was not pierced, and he ruled it kosher. Rav Ḥana objected with Levi's teaching that a bird whose skull is broken is a tereifa even if the membrane is intact. Rav Mattana answered that Levi meant a water bird, because its membrane is fragile.
why: The Gemara is asking whether a bird with a broken skull can be inspected and permitted, given Levi's teaching. The same objection and answer have just appeared between Rav Naḥman and Rav Anan; this case shows the answer applied to a real hen.

people.name: Rav Ḥana
people.about: Owner of the injured hen; he challenges Rav Mattana's ruling.

people.name: Rav Mattana
people.about: The Sage who inspected the hen and ruled it kosher.

people.name: Levi
people.about: A Sage whose teaching lists the defects that make a bird forbidden.

terms.meaning: The thin covering around the brain. If it is pierced, the bird is forbidden; the question is whether a broken skull alone is enough.
An animal or bird with a fatal defect; its meat is forbidden even if properly slaughtered.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the mishna, the core collection of Jewish law.

note: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi had a hen that fell into the fire. He sent it to Rabbi Elazar HaKappar, telling him its innards had turned green, and Rabbi Elazar HaKappar ruled it kosher. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi objected that the mishna says green innards make a bird unfit. Rabbi Elazar HaKappar answered that the rule applies only to the gizzard, the heart and the liver.
why: The mishna rules that a bird that fell into a fire is a tereifa if its innards turned green. This case limits that rule to the organs that are normally red, and the Gemara backs the answer with a baraita.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
people.about: Owner of the hen; he questions the ruling.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar HaKappar
people.about: Called 'the distinguished'; the Sage who ruled the hen kosher.

terms.meaning: Forbidden to eat because of a fatal defect, the status called tereifa.
A muscular stomach in birds that grinds food.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the mishna, the core collection of Jewish law.

note: Rabbi Yitzḥak bar Yosef had a hen that fell into the fire, and he sent it to Rabbi Abbahu. Its innards were red, yet it was ruled a tereifa. Rabbi Yitzḥak objected that the mishna says red innards are kosher. The answer was that red innards that turned green, and green innards that turned red, make a bird a tereifa; the mishna's rule that red is kosher applies only to the heart, the gizzard and the liver.
why: It is the companion to the case just told, where green innards were permitted. Together they show that the mishna's color test for a bird that fell into fire depends on each organ's natural color.

people.name: Rabbi Yitzḥak bar Yosef
people.about: Owner of the hen; he questions the ruling.

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: The Sage the hen was sent to.

terms.meaning: An animal or bird with a fatal defect; its meat is forbidden even if properly slaughtered.
The early collection of Jewish law on which the Gemara comments.

flag: The hen is sent to Rabbi Abbahu, but the English translation credits the ruling and answer to Rabbi Elazar HaKappar, which the Aramaic does not name; the note avoids naming who ruled.

note: A Roman saw a man fall from a roof to the ground; his belly burst open and his intestines came out. The Roman brought the man's son and slaughtered him in front of him, but only as an illusion. The father fainted and went limp, his intestines slipped back inside, and the Roman sewed up his belly.
why: The mishna says a bird whose intestines came out but were not pierced stays kosher, and a Sage adds that organs have fixed places and must go back in order. The story shows intestines returning to their place in a man.

people.name: the Roman
people.about: An unnamed Roman who stages the trick and sews up the injured man.

note: A young deer was brought to the house of the Exilarch, its hind legs cut. Rav examined the sinews of its thigh, found them intact and ruled it kosher, and he meant to eat it lightly roasted. Shmuel asked him whether he was not worried it might have been bitten by a snake. When Rav asked what could be done, Shmuel said to put it in a hot oven, where it would test itself. He did, and the meat fell off in pieces. Shmuel applied to Rav the verse 'No mischief shall befall the righteous,' and Rav applied to Shmuel the verse 'No secret causes you trouble.'
why: The mishna, as the Gemara cites it, says an animal bitten by a snake is not a tereifa but is still forbidden because it is dangerous. The incident shows how that danger was detected; it also follows a run of warnings about foods that harm the body.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage who inspected the deer, ruled it kosher and planned to eat it.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The Sage who suspected a snakebite and proposed the oven test.

terms.meaning: The head of the Jewish community in Babylonia, a powerful leader in whose household Sages often ate and ruled.
The place in the thigh where the tendons meet; if they are intact, an animal with injured legs can still be kosher.
Permitted to eat under Jewish law.

note: In the house of the Exilarch a karkoz goat was slaughtered, and a whole basket of fat was taken from it. Rav Aḥai declared the fat forbidden, but Rav Shmuel, son of Rabbi Abbahu, ate some of it and applied to himself the verse 'A man's belly shall be filled with the fruit of his mouth.' The Sages of the Land of Israel sent word that the law follows Rav Shmuel, son of Rabbi Abbahu, but that people should be mindful of Rav Aḥai's honor, because he lights up the eyes of the exile.
why: The Gemara has just set out the signs on the horns that mark an animal as wild, whose fat is permitted, rather than domesticated, whose fat is forbidden. The karkoz goat was the uncertain case those signs left open.

people.name: Rav Aḥai
people.about: The Sage who forbade the fat; the Sages of the Land of Israel praise him as one who lights up the eyes of the exile.

people.name: Rav Shmuel, son of Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: The Sage who ate the fat, trusting his own learning; the law was ruled to follow him.

terms.meaning: A kind of goat whose status was in doubt: was it a domesticated animal or a wild one?
Certain fats of domesticated animals such as cattle, sheep and goats are forbidden by the Torah; the same fats of wild animals are permitted.
The head of the Jewish community in Babylonia, in whose household this goat was slaughtered.

note: The Roman emperor told Rabbi Yehoshua ben Ḥananya that his God is compared to a lion, yet a horseman can kill a lion. Rabbi Yehoshua said God is compared to the lion of Bei Ila'ei. The emperor insisted on seeing it, so Rabbi Yehoshua prayed and the lion set out. Four hundred parasangs away it roared once: pregnant women miscarried and the wall of Rome fell. At three hundred it roared again: men's teeth fell out, and the emperor fell from his throne. He begged Rabbi Yehoshua to pray it back, and it returned. Another time the emperor asked to see God. Rabbi Yehoshua stood him facing the summer sun, and when he could not look, said: if you cannot look at one of God's servants, all the more so the Divine Presence.
why: Rav Yehuda has just identified an animal from a list of kosher and forbidden beasts as the lion of Bei Ila'ei, and Rav Kahana has described its enormous size. The story about that lion follows, and a second exchange with the same emperor is told after it.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Ḥananya
people.about: The Sage who answers the emperor's challenges and prays to bring the lion and send it back.

people.name: the emperor
people.about: The Roman emperor who mocks the comparison of God to a lion and demands to see first the lion, then God.

terms.meaning: A giant lion from a place called Bei Ila'ei; the Gemara says it measured nine cubits between its ears.
A Persian measure of distance, roughly four miles.
God's presence in the world, called the Shekhina.
A Hebrew month in midsummer, when the sun is at its strongest.

flag: The span joins two separate exchanges between the emperor and Rabbi Yehoshua (the lion of Bei Ila'ei, and the request to see God); each could stand as its own story.

note: The Roman emperor told Rabbi Yehoshua ben Ḥananya that he wanted to prepare a meal for his God. Rabbi Yehoshua said he could not, because God's hosts are too many. The emperor insisted, so Rabbi Yehoshua told him to set it out on the shore of the great sea, where there is open space. The emperor worked for the six months of summer, and a wind swept it all into the sea; he worked the six months of winter, and rain sank it all into the sea. When he asked what this was, Rabbi Yehoshua said these were only the sweepers and floor washers who serve God. The emperor admitted that he could not do it.
why: It is one of a series of exchanges between the Roman emperor and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Ḥananya that the Gemara strings together, each showing the emperor that God's greatness is beyond him.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Ḥananya
people.about: The Sage who tells the emperor how and where to prepare the meal.

people.name: the emperor
people.about: The Roman emperor who wants to host a meal for the God of Israel.

note: The Roman emperor's daughter told Rabbi Yehoshua ben Ḥananya that his God must be a carpenter, quoting a verse about God laying the beams of His upper chambers in the waters, and asked him to tell God to make her a distaff. He agreed and prayed, and she was struck with leprosy. She was seated in the Roman market and given a distaff, since Romans gave one to every leper so that people would see and pray for them. One day Rabbi Yehoshua passed by and asked whether she liked the distaff his God had given her. She told him to ask his God to take back what He had given. He replied that our God gives but does not take back.
why: It continues the run of exchanges between the Roman emperor's household and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Ḥananya, each turning a mocking challenge about God back on the one who made it.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Ḥananya
people.about: The Sage who prays for the emperor's daughter and later speaks with her in the market.

people.name: the emperor's daughter
people.about: The daughter of the Roman emperor, who mocks God as a carpenter and asks for a distaff.

terms.meaning: A simple stick used in spinning, holding the wool or flax that is drawn off into thread.
The translation's word for a serious skin disease; in Rome, according to the story, sufferers sat in the market to draw people's prayers.

note: Rav Naḥman bar Pappa had a garden. He planted seeds, but they did not sprout. He prayed, rain came, and they sprouted. He said that this is what Rav Asi had taught.
why: Rav Asi has just explained that the grass created on the third day waited at the surface until Adam prayed for rain, because God desires the prayers of the righteous. Rav Naḥman bar Pappa's garden is that teaching borne out in his own life.

people.name: Rav Naḥman bar Pappa
people.about: The Sage whose garden sprouted only after he prayed.

people.name: Rav Asi
people.about: The Sage whose teaching Rav Naḥman bar Pappa says his garden confirmed.

note: A bear attacked a ben pekua belonging to Adda bar Ḥavu, and he came to Rav Ashi, who told him to go and slaughter it. Adda bar Ḥavu objected that Ze'eiri, quoting Rabbi Ḥanina, rules like Rabbi Shimon Shezuri, who permits such an animal without slaughter, and that even Rabbi Yoḥanan disagreed only about its offspring. Rav Ashi said Rabbi Yoḥanan was only explaining Rabbi Shimon Shezuri's view. Adda bar Ḥavu pressed on with another report that the law follows Rabbi Shimon Shezuri wherever the Mishna quotes him. Rav Ashi said he holds with Rabbi Yonatan, who follows Rabbi Shimon Shezuri only for a man dangerously ill and for teruma of the tithe of demai.
why: The Gemara has just quoted Ze'eiri's ruling that a ben pekua needs no slaughter even after it has walked on the ground. This case shows Rav Ashi refusing to follow that ruling, and the Gemara then explains the two cases where he does follow Rabbi Shimon Shezuri.

people.name: Adda bar Ḥavu
people.about: Owner of the animal attacked by the bear; he argues with Rav Ashi's ruling.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: The Sage who tells Adda bar Ḥavu to slaughter the animal and defends that ruling.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon Shezuri
people.about: An early Sage who permits a ben pekua, and its offspring, without slaughter.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: A Sage whose statement about the offspring of a ben pekua the two argue over.

people.name: Rabbi Yonatan
people.about: The Sage whose limited acceptance of Rabbi Shimon Shezuri Rav Ashi adopts.

terms.meaning: A calf or lamb found alive inside its mother when she was slaughtered. Its mother's slaughter may make it permitted, so whether it needs its own slaughter is debated.
The portion of the Levites' tithe that had to be given to a priest.
Produce bought from someone who might not have separated the required tithes.

note: Ulla told Rav Naḥman of an incident he knew of: a young bird in the house of Rabbi Yitzḥak had a broken leg, where skin and flesh together covered the bone. Rabbi Yitzḥak brought it to Rabbi Yoḥanan, who ruled it kosher. Rav Naḥman replied that a young bird is different, because its skin is soft.
why: The Gemara is debating what Rabbi Yoḥanan ruled about a broken bone sticking out: whether skin counts together with flesh in covering most of it. Ulla offers this incident as his evidence, and Rav Naḥman pushes it aside.

people.name: Ulla
people.about: The Sage who reports the incident as the source for his account of Rabbi Yoḥanan's ruling.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: The Sage who challenges Ulla and dismisses the incident as a special case.

people.name: Rabbi Yitzḥak
people.about: Owner of the young bird; he brought it to Rabbi Yoḥanan.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: The Sage who ruled the young bird kosher.

terms.meaning: Permitted to eat under Jewish law; here, not made forbidden by the broken leg.

note: An animal's leg bone broke and stuck out, and a small piece of it had come away. The case came before Abaye, who put off answering until three pilgrimage festivals had passed. Rav Adda bar Mattana told the owner to go to Rava, son of Rav Yosef bar Ḥama, whose knife is sharp. The owner went, and Rava said: since the rule speaks of a bone that broke and stuck out, what difference does it make whether a piece fell off or stayed in place?
why: The Gemara is working through a baraita that permits an animal whose broken bone sticks out, as long as skin and flesh cover most of it. This case asks whether a missing chip of bone changes that, and Rava's answer treats it as the same.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: The Sage the case first came to; he delayed for three festivals.

people.name: Rav Adda bar Mattana
people.about: The Sage who sent the owner to Rava.

people.name: Rava, son of Rav Yosef bar Ḥama
people.about: A Sage described as having a sharp knife, quick and incisive in ruling; he decides the case.

terms.meaning: Passover, Shavuot and Sukkot, when crowds gathered; Abaye waited for them so he could ask the assembled Sages.
An idiom for a scholar who cuts through legal questions quickly and decisively.

note: Moths got into Rabbi Hiyya's flax, and he came to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi for advice. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi told him to slaughter a bird over the tub of water where the flax was soaking: the moths would smell the blood and leave. The Gemara asks how this was allowed, since a baraita says that one who slaughters because he needs the blood must still cover it. Two traditions answer: Rav Dimi reported that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi told him first to make the bird a tereifa and then slaughter it, and Ravin reported that he told him to tear loose its windpipe and gullet instead of slaughtering it.
why: The mishna says one who stabs an animal or tears loose its windpipe and gullet need not cover the blood; this case shows that rule put to practical use, and the Gemara goes on to ask why Rav Dimi's version did not simply say to tear the organs loose.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: A Sage whose flax was infested with moths; he asked Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi what to do.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called simply Rabbi; he advised using a bird's blood to drive the moths away.

people.name: Rav Dimi
people.about: A Sage who came from Eretz Yisrael and reported one version of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's instruction.

people.name: Ravin
people.about: A Sage who came from Eretz Yisrael and reported a second version of the instruction.

terms.meaning: A Torah commandment: when a wild animal or bird is slaughtered, its blood must be covered with earth rather than left exposed or used.
An animal or bird with a fatal injury or defect; it is forbidden to eat even if properly slaughtered, and slaughtering it does not require covering the blood.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna but is quoted in the Gemara as an authority.

note: Rabbi Abba, son of Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba, and Rabbi Zeira were standing in the marketplace of Caesarea at the door of the study hall. Rabbi Ami came out, found them, and scolded them: had he not told them not to stand outside while the study hall was in session, in case someone inside needed help with a point of law? Rabbi Zeira went in; Rabbi Abba did not. Inside, the students were puzzling over which of two rulings by Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi was the later one, and Rabbi Zeira complained that they had not told him while he was outside, so he could have asked the elder, Rabbi Abba, who might have heard the answer from his father, who reviewed his learning before Rabbi Yohanan every thirty days.
why: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi ruled once like Rabbi Meir and once like the Rabbis on slaughtering the offspring of an animal slaughtered by a deaf-mute, imbecile or minor; the Gemara asks which ruling came later, and this incident shows the question was asked but left open.

people.name: Rabbi Abba, son of Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba
people.about: Called the elder here; he stayed outside the study hall and might have known the answer from his father.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: Stood outside with Rabbi Abba, then went into the study hall when scolded.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: Came out of the study hall and rebuked the two for standing outside during study.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba
people.about: Rabbi Abba's father, who reviewed his studies before Rabbi Yohanan every thirty days.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: The teacher before whom Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba reviewed his learning.

terms.meaning: The house of study where Sages and students gathered to learn and debate Jewish law.
Jewish law; here, a specific legal ruling someone might need explained.

note: Rav Beruna and Rav Hananel, students of Rav, were sitting at a meal while Rav Yeiva the Elder stood over them serving. They asked him for a cup of wine over which to recite Grace after Meals, then changed their minds and asked for a cup to drink. Rav Yeiva the Elder told them that Rav had said: once a person says 'Give me a cup to say the blessing,' he is forbidden to drink more wine, because he has declared his meal over.
why: Rabbi Hanina says even Rabbi Yehuda, who requires covering a wild animal's blood before slaughtering a bird, allows one blessing for both. This incident is raised to argue the pause needs a new blessing; the Gemara rejects it, since one can slaughter with one hand and cover with the other.

people.name: Rav Beruna
people.about: A student of Rav, dining with Rav Hananel.

people.name: Rav Hananel
people.about: A student of Rav, dining with Rav Beruna.

people.name: Rav Yeiva the Elder
people.about: Served the two students at their meal and told them Rav's rule about the cup of blessing.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The teacher of the two students, whose ruling Rav Yeiva quotes.

terms.meaning: The blessings said at the end of a meal with bread, often recited over a cup of wine.

note: A heretic told Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi that the verse 'He Who forms the mountains and He Who creates the wind' shows two separate gods. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi called him an imbecile and pointed to the verse's end: 'The Lord, the God of hosts, is His name.' The heretic asked for three days to find a rebuttal, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi fasted those three days. As he sat down to eat, he was told a heretic was at the door. It was another heretic, who said the first had found no answer, thrown himself from the roof and died. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi invited him to dine, then offered him the cup of blessing or forty gold coins. He chose the cup, and a Divine Voice declared the cup of blessing worth forty gold coins. Rabbi Yitzhak says the man's family, bar Luyyanus, is still prominent in Rome.
why: Rabban Gamliel fined a man ten gold coins for taking another's mitzva of covering blood, and the Gemara asks whether the fine pays for the mitzva or for its blessing. The Divine Voice's forty coins for a four-blessing Grace after Meals suggests ten coins per blessing.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called simply Rabbi; he answered the heretic's argument from the verse and fasted while awaiting his rebuttal.

people.name: Rabbi Yitzhak
people.about: A Sage who reports that the second heretic's family still exists among the prominent families of Rome.

terms.meaning: Here, someone who argued against the Jewish belief in one God, using verses of the Bible to claim there were several gods.
The cup of wine over which Grace after Meals is recited; the one who leads the blessing holds it and drinks from it.
A voice from Heaven that, in rabbinic stories, announces God's view of an event.

note: Rav Yehuda bar Oshaya was peeling the membranes off a spleen for Levi, son of Rav Huna bar Hiyya, cutting them only from the upper surface. Levi told him to go down further. Levi's father, Rav Huna bar Hiyya, came in, found him saying this, and told him that his own mother's father, Rav Yirmeya bar Abba, had said in the name of Rav that the Torah forbids only the membranes on the thick, upper surface of the spleen.
why: The Gemara has just listed the membranes forbidden for eating, including the spleen's because it contains forbidden fat; this incident asks how much of that membrane is forbidden, and Levi goes on to challenge his father with a baraita.

people.name: Rav Yehuda bar Oshaya
people.about: Was preparing a spleen for Levi by peeling off its membranes.

people.name: Levi
people.about: Son of Rav Huna bar Hiyya; he told Rav Yehuda bar Oshaya to cut deeper.

people.name: Rav Huna bar Hiyya
people.about: Levi's father, who corrected him by quoting Levi's maternal grandfather.

people.name: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba
people.about: Levi's mother's father, who transmitted a ruling in the name of Rav.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage in whose name the ruling about the spleen's membranes was given.

terms.meaning: Thin layers of tissue on the spleen that the Sages considered forbidden fat, so they had to be removed before the meat could be eaten.

note: Shmuel was crossing a river on a ferry. He told his attendant to give the ferryman a suitable gift as payment. The attendant did so, and Shmuel became angry with him. The story itself does not say why.
why: The Gemara is explaining why a Jew may not send a gentile a cut-up thigh with its sciatic nerve still in it: it would deceive him, and Shmuel forbade deceiving even a gentile. That ruling, the Gemara says, was inferred from this incident, and it then debates what Shmuel was angry about.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: A Sage who was crossing a river by ferry and became angry at how his attendant paid the ferryman.

terms.meaning: A Sage's personal servant or student who carried out errands for him.

note: A man sent a friend a barrel of wine with a layer of oil floating on top, so it looked like a barrel of oil. The friend, thinking he had oil, invited guests to share it. When they arrived and he found the barrel was wine, he hanged himself in his shame.
why: A baraita is listing ways one may not mislead others, such as passing off a dead animal's hide as a slaughtered one's; it rules that one may not send wine with oil floating on top, and this incident shows the harm such a deception can do.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna but is quoted in the Gemara as an authority.

note: In years of famine a man invited three guests but had only three eggs to set before them. His son came in, and each guest in turn gave the boy his portion. The father came and found the boy with one egg in his mouth and two in his hand, and struck him to the ground, and the boy died. When the mother saw, she went up to the roof, fell and died, and the father too went up to the roof, fell and died. Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov said that three Jewish souls were killed over this matter.
why: A baraita rules that guests may not give their host's son or daughter food from their plates without the host's permission; this incident is its warning. The Gemara notes that Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's comment shows the whole baraita is his.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
people.about: A Sage who said three Jewish souls were killed over guests giving food to a host's child.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna but is quoted in the Gemara as an authority.

note: Mar Zutra, son of Rav Nahman, was traveling from Sikhra to Bei Mehoza when he met Rava and Rav Safra heading toward Sikhra. Thinking they had come out to greet him, he asked why the Rabbis had troubled themselves to come so far. Rav Safra told him they had not known he was coming, and would have gone to more trouble if they had. Afterward Rava asked Rav Safra why he had said this and upset Mar Zutra. Rav Safra answered that otherwise they would have misled him, and Rava replied that Mar Zutra had misled himself.
why: Butchers announced a tereifa for gentiles only as 'meat for the soldiers'; the Gemara answers the charge that this deceives them by saying they deceive themselves, and this incident proves that letting someone mislead himself is permitted.

people.name: Mar Zutra, son of Rav Nahman
people.about: Was traveling to Bei Mehoza and assumed the two Sages had come out to greet him.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Was traveling with Rav Safra; he faulted Rav Safra for upsetting Mar Zutra.

people.name: Rav Safra
people.about: Told Mar Zutra frankly that they had not come out to greet him.

note: A Jewish butcher told another man that if he had made peace with him, he would have given him a cut from the fattened bull he prepared the day before. The man replied that he had eaten the finest of it anyway, since a certain gentile had bought some and fed it to him. The butcher said he had prepared two bulls, and the one the man ate was a tereifa. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi asked whether, because of this imbecile who acted improperly, they should forbid all the meat in the butcher shops. Others report that he said the butcher only meant to cause his fellow distress.
why: The Gemara has been discussing selling non-kosher meat to gentiles. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's reaction fits his ruling that meat found with a gentile is permitted where the butchers are Jewish, and the Gemara goes on to ask why, in the second version, his ruling rests on the butcher's spite.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called simply Rabbi; he refused to forbid all the butcher shops because of this one butcher.

terms.meaning: An animal with a fatal injury or defect; its meat is not kosher even if it was properly slaughtered.
An ox specially fed to be fat, prized for its meat.

note: Rav was sitting at the ford of the Ishtetit River when he saw a man cleaning an animal's head in the water. The head fell from his hands, so he brought a basket, cast it into the river and pulled out two heads. Rav asked whether it commonly happens that one loses one thing and finds two, and forbade both heads to him. Rav Kahana and Rav Asi asked Rav whether forbidden meat is common and permitted meat not, and he answered that forbidden meat is more common.
why: The Gemara has been testing Rav's view that meat out of one's sight becomes forbidden; it explains that he never stated this outright, and the rule was inferred from this incident. It then asks whether the incident proves much, since that spot was a port of gentiles.

people.name: Rav
people.about: A Sage who watched the man fish two animal heads out of the river and forbade both.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: Questioned Rav's ruling together with Rav Asi.

people.name: Rav Asi
people.about: Questioned Rav's ruling together with Rav Kahana.

terms.meaning: A shallow place where a river can be crossed; here, a spot on the riverbank where people came to wash things.

note: Rav was traveling to the home of his son-in-law, Rav Hanan, and saw the ferry coming toward him just as he arrived; he said this meant a good day awaited him where he was going. At Rav Hanan's gate he looked through a crack in the door and saw an animal hanging, ready to be cooked. He knocked, and everyone came out to greet him, the butchers too, while Rav never took his eyes off the meat. He told them that if they had relied on their own watching just then, they would have fed forbidden meat to his daughter's sons. Even so, Rav did not eat from that meat.
why: The Gemara has asked how Rav ever ate meat, given his view that meat left out of sight becomes forbidden. Here he kept it in sight himself, so the Gemara asks why he still refused it: perhaps for treating the ferry as an omen, or because it was an optional feast.

people.name: Rav
people.about: A Sage visiting his son-in-law; he kept watch over the meat but did not eat it.

people.name: Rav Hanan
people.about: Rav's son-in-law, at whose home the meal was being prepared.

terms.meaning: A boat carrying travelers across a river; Rav took its arrival just as he reached the bank as a good sign.

note: As long as Rav lived, Rabbi Yohanan in Eretz Yisrael addressed his letters 'To our Master who is in Babylonia.' After Rav died, he wrote to Shmuel as 'our colleague in Babylonia.' Shmuel, stung, sent him the calculation of leap years for the next sixty years, but Rabbi Yohanan said this only showed he knew arithmetic. Then Shmuel sent him rulings on doubtful cases of tereifot that filled thirteen camel loads, and Rabbi Yohanan said: I have a Master in Babylonia; I will go and see him. Before setting out he asked a child to recite his verse, and the child said, 'Now Samuel was dead.' Rabbi Yohanan concluded that Shmuel had died, and did not go.
why: The Gemara has just said that Rabbi Yohanan would seek a sign by asking a child for his verse; this is an example. The Gemara then adds that Shmuel had not died; the sign came so Rabbi Yohanan would be spared the hard journey.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: A Sage in Eretz Yisrael who wrote letters to the leading Sages of Babylonia.

people.name: Rav
people.about: A Sage in Babylonia whom Rabbi Yohanan addressed as 'our Master' while he lived.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: A Sage in Babylonia who set out to prove to Rabbi Yohanan that he was his master.

terms.meaning: Years in which an extra month is added to the Jewish calendar so the lunar months stay in step with the seasons; working them out required expert calculation.
Plural of tereifa: animals with a fatal injury or defect, whose meat is not kosher; deciding doubtful cases takes great expertise.

note: A man called bar Peyoli was standing before Shmuel, removing the sciatic nerve from an animal's leg, cutting it out without scraping away the surrounding flesh. Shmuel told him to go down further, and said that if he had not been watching, bar Peyoli would have fed him forbidden meat. Bar Peyoli was so frightened that the knife fell from his hand. Shmuel told him not to be afraid: whoever taught him had taught him in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda.
why: The mishna records a dispute: the first view requires scraping away flesh to remove the whole sciatic nerve, while Rabbi Yehuda says cutting it out is enough. This incident opens the Gemara's discussion, with Shmuel following the first view, and Rav Sheshet then asks which part bar Peyoli had left.

people.name: bar Peyoli
people.about: A man removing the sciatic nerve from a leg of meat in front of Shmuel.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: A Sage who corrected bar Peyoli's work and then reassured him.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: A Sage of the mishna whose more lenient method bar Peyoli had been taught.

terms.meaning: A nerve in an animal's hind leg that the Torah forbids eating, in memory of Jacob's injury when he wrestled the angel; it must be cut out before the meat is eaten.

note: In the home of the Exilarch, some animal thighs were salted with the sciatic nerve still inside. Ravina ruled the meat forbidden, and Rav Aha bar Rav Ashi ruled it permitted. They went and asked Mar bar Rav Ashi, who told them: My father permitted it.
why: Shmuel ruled that a thigh cooked with its sciatic nerve is entirely forbidden, but a roasted one may be eaten once the nerve is reached. The question is whether salting counts as cooking, and the Gemara goes on to show Ravina's strict ruling is hard to square with Shmuel.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: A Sage who ruled the salted thighs forbidden.

people.name: Rav Aha bar Rav Ashi
people.about: A Sage who ruled the salted thighs permitted.

people.name: Mar bar Rav Ashi
people.about: Was asked to decide, and reported that his father permitted such meat.

terms.meaning: The head of the Jewish community in Babylonia, a hereditary leader recognized by the government.
A nerve in an animal's hind leg that the Torah forbids eating; it must be removed before the meat is eaten.

note: Half an olive-bulk of forbidden fat fell into a pot of kosher meat. Mar bar Rav Ashi thought it would be enough for the meat to be thirty half-olive-bulks, half the usual ratio. His father, Rav Ashi, said to him: Have I not told you not to treat measures lightly, even rabbinic ones? He added that Rabbi Yohanan said even a half-measure is forbidden by Torah law, so the fat is cancelled only by sixty times its volume of meat.
why: The Gemara is discussing how forbidden food that falls into a mixture is cancelled, generally by sixty times its volume; just before, Rav Ashi was challenged over measuring with what the pot had absorbed, and this second incident about the measure follows.

people.name: Mar bar Rav Ashi
people.about: Son of Rav Ashi; he wanted to use a smaller measure to cancel the fat.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Mar bar Rav Ashi's father, who rebuked him for treating measures lightly.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: A Sage quoted by Rav Ashi: even half the forbidden amount is prohibited by Torah law.

terms.meaning: A standard measure of volume, about the size of an olive; it is the smallest amount of forbidden food for which one is punished.
Certain fats of cattle, sheep and goats that the Torah forbids eating.
Less than the minimum amount that brings punishment; Rabbi Yohanan holds that eating it is still forbidden by the Torah.

note: A man came before Rabbi Hanina with a question while Rabbi Yehuda bar Zevina sat at the gate. When the man came out, Rabbi Yehuda bar Zevina asked what Rabbi Hanina had said, and the man said he had permitted it. Rabbi Yehuda bar Zevina told him to bring it before Rabbi Hanina again. Rabbi Hanina said: Who is this who is bothering me? Go tell the one sitting at the gate that sciatic nerves do not impart flavor.
why: The mishna measures whether a sciatic nerve cooked in a thigh flavors the meat, while a baraita cites the view that nerves impart no flavor at all; this incident shows Rabbi Hanina ruling by that view, which the Gemara adopts as the law.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina
people.about: A Sage who permitted the man's meat and sent word that sciatic nerves do not impart flavor.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda bar Zevina
people.about: Was sitting at the gate and sent the man back to Rabbi Hanina to ask again.

terms.meaning: A nerve in an animal's hind leg that the Torah forbids eating; it must be removed before the meat is eaten.
A forbidden food cooked with permitted food makes the mixture forbidden only if its taste passes into it; if nerves have no taste, the rest of the meat stays permitted.

note: Rav Yitzhak, son of Rav Mesharshiyya, visited the house of Rav Ashi. They brought him cheese and he ate it, then brought him meat and he ate it without washing his hands in between. The household objected that Agra had taught only that bird meat and cheese may be eaten freely, which implies that meat of cattle and cheese may not. Rav Yitzhak answered that Agra's rule applies at night, but by day he can see that nothing is left on his hands.
why: The Gemara has just quoted Agra, father-in-law of Rabbi Abba, that bird meat and cheese may be eaten without washing hands or wiping the mouth between them; this incident limits that teaching.

people.name: Rav Yitzhak, son of Rav Mesharshiyya
people.about: A visitor at Rav Ashi's house who ate meat after cheese without washing his hands.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: The Sage whose household served Rav Yitzhak and questioned what he did.

people.name: Agra
people.about: Father-in-law of Rabbi Abba, whose teaching about bird meat and cheese the household quoted.

terms.meaning: Jewish law forbids eating meat and dairy together, so the Sages discuss what must be done, such as washing hands, between eating one and the other.

note: Abaye would inspect his property every day. One day he met his sharecropper carrying a load of wood and asked where he was taking it. The sharecropper said: To the Master's house. Abaye, knowing the man meant to keep the wood for himself, told him: The Sages already got there before you.
why: Shmuel has just said that one who inspects his property every day will find a coin, meaning it will pay off; Abaye's encounter shows that advice at work.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage who inspected his property every day and caught his sharecropper with the wood.

terms.meaning: A tenant who farms another person's land in exchange for a share of the crop.

note: Rav Asi inspected his property every day and asked where were all the coins that Mar Shmuel had promised. One day he saw a water channel that had burst and was flooding his land. He took off his cloak, rolled it up and stuffed it into the gap, then shouted, and people came and sealed the hole. He said: I have found all of Mar Shmuel's coins.
why: Shmuel has said that one who inspects his property every day will find an asteira coin; after Abaye's story, this is a second case showing that the daily check pays off.

people.name: Rav Asi
people.about: A Sage who inspected his property daily and doubted it was worth it, until he found the flood.

people.name: Mar Shmuel
people.about: The Sage who taught that inspecting one's property every day will turn up a coin.

terms.meaning: A small coin; Shmuel's saying means that regular checks on one's property bring a reward.

note: The ministering angel of poverty kept pursuing a certain man but could never get hold of him, because the man was exceptionally careful to gather up his crumbs. One day the man broke his bread over grass, and the angel said: Now he will certainly fall into my hands. But after eating, the man took a hoe, uprooted the grass and threw it into the river. Then he heard the angel say: Woe, that man has removed me from my house.
why: Abaye has just reported learning from his teacher that people gather crumbs after a meal not for cleanliness but because leaving them invites poverty; this tale shows that belief in action.

people.name: the ministering angel of poverty
people.about: A spirit that pursues the man, trying to make him poor.

terms.meaning: In rabbinic tradition, a heavenly being assigned to a particular task or domain; here, one whose job is to bring poverty.
