note: Rav Ḥisda and Rabba bar Rav Huna were traveling on a boat when a certain matron asked them to seat her with them. They refused. She said an incantation and bound the boat so it could not move; they said something of their own and released it. She told them: What can I do to you? You do not wipe yourselves with an earthenware shard, you do not kill a louse on your clothes, and you do not eat vegetables from a bundle tied by the gardener.
why: Abaye has just said his teacher told him that eating vegetables from a gardener's tied bundle exposes one to witchcraft; the witch's own words confirm that avoiding it protected these Sages.

people.name: Rav Ḥisda
people.about: One of two Sages traveling on the boat who refuse the matron a seat.

people.name: Rabba bar Rav Huna
people.about: His fellow traveler on the boat.

people.name: the matron
people.about: A woman who asks to sit with the Sages and, when refused, uses witchcraft against them.

terms.meaning: The translation's word for a woman of standing, usually a non-Jewish noblewoman; here she is a practitioner of witchcraft.

note: Some porters carrying a barrel of wine set it down to rest under a gutter, and it burst. They came to Mar bar Rav Ashi, who had horns blown and excommunicated the demon of that place. The demon came and complained that the porters had put the barrel on its ear. Mar bar Rav Ashi answered that a demon has no business in a busy place, so it was in the wrong and must pay. The demon asked for a deadline, came late, and explained that demons cannot take anything tied up, sealed, measured or counted, and must wait until they find something ownerless.
why: Abaye has just said his teacher told him people avoid sitting under a gutter because demons are found there; this story shows a demon living under one.

people.name: Mar bar Rav Ashi
people.about: The Sage the porters turn to; he summons the demon, judges it and orders it to pay.

people.name: the demon
people.about: A spirit living under the gutter that burst the porters' barrel.

terms.meaning: Placed under a formal ban by a Sage, a serious sanction that cuts someone off from the community; here, remarkably, applied to a demon, with horns blown as part of the ceremony.
Property that belongs to no one, which anyone may take. The demon says this is the only kind of thing demons are permitted to take.

note: A son of a demon served in Rav Pappa's household. Sent to fetch water from the river, it was slow to return, and when asked why, it said it had waited for the foul waters to pass. Then it saw the household pouring a little water out of the mouth of the pitcher before drinking, and said: Had I known you do this, I would not have delayed.
why: Abaye has just said his teacher explained that people pour off water from a pitcher's mouth before drinking because of foul waters; the demon's remark confirms the reason.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: A Sage whose household had the son of a demon as a servant.

people.name: the son of a demon
people.about: A demon's offspring serving in Rav Pappa's house, who fetches water from the river.

terms.meaning: Water thought to be harmful or contaminated by evil forces at certain times; the household's practice of pouring off the top of the pitcher was meant to get rid of it.

note: Rav Dimi, arriving from the Land of Israel, reported that failing to wash with the first waters, before a meal, once led to a Jew being fed pig meat. As the translation explains the incident, a storekeeper sold different meat to Jews and gentiles; when a Jewish customer did not wash before eating, the storekeeper took him for a gentile and served him pork.
why: The discussion turns from demons to handwashing at meals; Rav Dimi's report is the first half of a pair of cautionary tales about neglecting the washing before and after eating.

people.name: Rav Dimi
people.about: A Sage who came from the Land of Israel and reported this incident.

terms.meaning: The ritual washing of hands before eating bread. Its counterpart, the final waters, is the washing after the meal.

flag: The Hebrew of the story is a single clause of Rav Dimi's two-part saying; the incident itself comes only from the translator's explanation, and the second half (the final waters) falls in the next segment.

note: Failing to wash with the final waters, after a meal, once led to a woman being divorced from her husband. As the translation tells it, a host who had stolen his guests' money still had lentils on his mustache; the guests told his wife that her husband wanted their money returned and gave the lentils he had eaten as proof. She gave it back, and he divorced her in anger. Ravin, also from the Land of Israel, told it differently: the first waters fed a Jew carcass meat, and the final waters killed a person. Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak gave a way to remember it: Rav Dimi came and divorced her; Ravin came and killed her.
why: The Gemara is stressing the washing of hands before and after meals; these tales, in two versions, show the harm that came from skipping it.

people.name: Ravin
people.about: A Sage who came from the Land of Israel and reported a harsher version of the incidents.

people.name: Rav Dimi
people.about: The Sage whose version said the woman was divorced.

people.name: Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak
people.about: Offers a memory aid to keep the two versions apart.

terms.meaning: The washing of hands, and here also the mouth, after a meal. Had the host washed, there would have been no lentils on his mustache to betray what he ate.
Meat of an animal that died without proper ritual slaughter, which Jews may not eat.

flag: Starts mid-saying: the first half of Rav Dimi's statement is in the preceding segment, and the incident details come only from the translator's explanation.

note: Shmuel found Rav eating with a cloth over his hands and asked him: Do we act this way? Rav answered that he was delicate, which the translation explains as meaning he had washed his hands but did not like to hold food in his bare hands.
why: The Gemara is asking whether someone may eat with a cloth over his hands instead of washing; this exchange is offered as proof, though Rav's answer suggests he had washed after all.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: A Sage who finds Rav eating with a cloth and questions him.

people.name: Rav
people.about: A Sage who explains he uses the cloth because he is delicate.

terms.meaning: Holding bread through a napkin so the hands never touch it, raised here as a possible substitute for the ritual washing of hands before a meal.

note: When Rabbi Zeira moved from Babylonia to the Land of Israel, he found Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi eating with worn pieces of wineskin over their hands instead of washing. He asked how two great men could misread the case of Rav and Shmuel, since Rav had said he used a cloth only because he was delicate. The Gemara notes that Rabbi Zeira had forgotten Shmuel's ruling that the cloth is allowed for priests eating teruma, and Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi were priests.
why: Continuing the question of eating with a cloth instead of washing, this story shows a limited permission: the Gemara explains it applies to priests, who are careful not to touch their food.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: A Sage newly arrived from Babylonia who challenges the two rabbis.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: A Sage, a priest, found eating with his hands covered.

people.name: Rabbi Asi
people.about: A Sage, a priest, eating with Rabbi Ami.

terms.meaning: The portion of produce given to priests, which must be eaten in a state of ritual purity.
Descendants of Aaron, the kohanim, who were especially careful about purity when eating.

note: Shmuel's father found the young Shmuel crying. Shmuel said his teacher had struck him for feeding the teacher's son without washing his hands. Shmuel had asked: He is the one eating, and I must wash? His father said: Is it not enough that your teacher did not learn the law properly, that he strikes you too? The Gemara then rules that one who eats while being fed must wash, but the one feeding need not.
why: The Gemara is asking whether someone who feeds another must wash his hands; this incident supports the view that he need not, and the Gemara draws its ruling from it.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: A boy here, struck by his teacher for feeding the teacher's son without washing.

people.name: Shmuel's father
people.about: Finds his son crying and sides with him against the teacher.

note: Yalta said to her husband Rav Naḥman that for everything the Torah forbids it allows something similar: blood is forbidden but liver is allowed, a menstruating wife is forbidden but blood of purity after childbirth is not, pork is forbidden but a certain fish brain tastes like it, another man's wife is forbidden but a divorcee may remarry in her first husband's lifetime, and so on. So, she said, I want to eat something that tastes like meat cooked in milk. Rav Naḥman told his cooks to roast udders on a spit for her. The Gemara asks why they were not torn first, and answers that tearing is needed only when cooking in a pot.
why: The Gemara is discussing how an udder, full of milk, may be prepared; Rav Naḥman's order to roast it untorn shows that tearing is required only for pot-cooking.

people.name: Yalta
people.about: Rav Naḥman's wife, who argues for a permitted dish with the taste of meat and milk.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: Her husband, who has his cooks roast udders for her.

terms.meaning: Bleeding during a set period after childbirth that, by Torah law, does not make a woman ritually impure, so she remains permitted to her husband.
The widow of a man who died childless, whom his brother may marry, although a brother's wife is otherwise forbidden.
The Torah's term for a woman captured in war, whom a soldier may marry under set conditions (Deuteronomy 21).
An udder is meat that holds milk. The mishna requires tearing it open to drain the milk before cooking.

note: When Rav came to Tatlefush, he heard one woman ask another how much milk is needed to cook a quarter of meat. Rav concluded that the people there had not learned that meat cooked in milk is forbidden, so he stayed on and forbade them even udders.
why: Rav Yitzḥak bar Avudimi has just said no one taught Rav that udders are forbidden; Rav made the rule himself as a fence. This story shows why he did so.

people.name: Rav
people.about: A Sage who, visiting Tatlefush, forbids udders to the townspeople.

terms.meaning: The Torah forbids cooking a kid in its mother's milk; the Sages read this as a ban on cooking or eating meat and dairy together.

note: Ravin and Rav Yitzḥak bar Yosef visited Rav Pappi's house and were served a dish made of udder. Rav Yitzḥak bar Yosef ate; Ravin did not. Abaye said: Bereaved Ravin, why do you not eat? Rav Pappi's wife is the daughter of Rabbi Yitzḥak Nappaḥa, a master of good deeds; had she not learned in her father's house that this is allowed, she would not have made it.
why: The Gemara has been recording different views on whether udders may be eaten; this story shows one Sage eating and one holding back, and Abaye relying on the household's learning.

people.name: Ravin
people.about: A Sage who declines to eat the udder dish.

people.name: Rav Yitzḥak bar Yosef
people.about: A Sage visiting with Ravin, who eats the dish.

people.name: Rav Pappi
people.about: Their host.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage who questions Ravin's refusal.

people.name: Rabbi Yitzḥak Nappaḥa
people.about: Father of Rav Pappi's wife, called a master of good deeds.

terms.meaning: Abaye's sharp way of addressing Ravin; it works here as a rebuke for refusing the dish, not as a statement about his family.

note: In Sura people did not eat udders; in Pumbedita they did. Rami bar Tamrei of Pumbedita came to Sura on the eve of Yom Kippur, gathered the udders everyone threw away, and ate them. He was brought before Rav Ḥisda, and had an answer for every challenge: he ate outside the town limits; the grape seeds he roasted them on were over a year old, so neither idolatrous wine nor stolen; he wore no phylacteries because of intestinal illness and no fringes because his robe was borrowed. Meanwhile a man who did not honor his parents was tied up to be flogged, and Rami said to let him go, since a mitzva whose reward is stated beside it is not enforced by the court. Rav Ḥisda said: I see you are very sharp. Rami replied: In Rav Yehuda's town I would show you my sharpness.
why: The Gemara has been tracing local customs about udders; this story shows a traveler from a permissive town defending his custom in a strict one.

people.name: Rami bar Tamrei
people.about: Also called Rami bar Dikulei; a man from Pumbedita who eats udders in Sura and defends each of his actions.

people.name: Rav Ḥisda
people.about: The Sage in Sura before whom Rami is brought, who questions him.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: The Sage of Pumbedita whose rulings Rami cites.

terms.meaning: The rule that a traveler keeps the stricter customs of both his home town and the town he is visiting.
Wine poured in idol worship, which Jews may not use or benefit from in any way.
When owners have given up hope of recovering lost property, it is treated as ownerless and may be taken.
Tefillin: small leather boxes holding Torah verses, worn on the arm and head; they require a clean body.

note: Rabba bar Rav Huna visited the house of Rabba bar Rav Naḥman for Shabbat and was served three se'a of fine kneaded bread. He asked: Did you know I was coming? They answered: Are you more important to us than Shabbat? Scripture says, call Shabbat a delight. Meanwhile he found a liver with an artery full of blood and asked why they had prepared it so. They asked what they should do, and he told them to tear it lengthwise and widthwise and roast it with the cut facing down.
why: The Gemara is discussing how liver, full of blood, must be prepared; Rabba bar Rav Huna's instruction to tear it and turn the cut down shows the practice.

people.name: Rabba bar Rav Huna
people.about: A Sage visiting for Shabbat, who corrects how the liver was prepared.

people.name: Rabba bar Rav Naḥman
people.about: His host.

terms.meaning: A large measure of volume; three se'a is a lavish amount of bread.
A verse from Isaiah 58:13, taken as a command to honor the Sabbath with fine food.

note: Rav Ashi came to the house of his father-in-law, Rami bar Abba, and saw Rami's son skewering liver on top of meat to roast it. Rav Ashi said: How haughty is this Sage! Granted the Sages allowed it after the fact, did they say one may do it from the start?
why: Mareimar has just ruled that liver roasted above meat is allowed after the fact but should not be done from the start; Rav Ashi's rebuke applies that ruling.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: The visitor who rebukes his brother-in-law.

people.name: Rami bar Abba
people.about: Rav Ashi's father-in-law, at whose house this happens.

people.name: the son of Rami bar Abba
people.about: Roasts liver above meat; Rav Ashi calls him haughty.

terms.meaning: A legal phrase: something acceptable once done, though it should not be done in the first place (ab initio).

note: Rav visited the house of his grandson, Rav Shimi bar Ḥiyya. His eyes hurt, so they made him an ointment in an earthenware bowl; later they served him food in the same bowl. Rav tasted the ointment in the food and said: It imparts so much flavor! The Gemara says this is not a fair inference about Rav's view, since that ointment was especially bitter.
why: Rav and Shmuel disagree over a hot fish put in a meat bowl: does flavor passed second-hand still count? The Gemara says Rav's strict view was only inferred from this incident, and then questions the inference.

people.name: Rav
people.about: A Sage who tastes the ointment in his food.

people.name: Rav Shimi bar Ḥiyya
people.about: Rav's grandson, his host.

terms.meaning: The principle that a forbidden food's taste passing into another food can forbid it. The question here is about taste passed on second-hand, through a bowl.

note: Rabbi Elazar was attending Shmuel when Shmuel was served a hot fish placed in a meat bowl, and ate it with kutaḥ, a dairy dip. Shmuel offered him some, but Rabbi Elazar would not eat. Shmuel said: I gave it to your teacher and he ate, and you will not? Rabbi Elazar went to Rav and asked whether he had changed his ruling. Rav said: God forbid that the descendant of Abba bar Abba, meaning Shmuel, would feed me something I do not hold permitted.
why: Rav forbids and Shmuel permits eating a fish from a meat bowl with dairy; here the dispute plays out at the table, with Rav denying Shmuel's claim that he had eaten it.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar
people.about: A student of Rav, attending Shmuel, who refuses the dish.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: Called Mar Shmuel; eats the fish with kutaḥ and offers it to Rabbi Elazar.

people.name: Rav
people.about: Rabbi Elazar's teacher, who says Shmuel would not have fed him what he forbids.

terms.meaning: A Babylonian dip or condiment made with milk, so a dairy food.
Shmuel's father. Rav refers to Shmuel as his descendant.

note: Rav Huna and Rav Ḥiyya bar Ashi sat eating on opposite sides of the ford of Sura. One was served a fish placed in a meat bowl and ate it with kutaḥ; the other was served figs and grapes during the meal and ate them without a blessing. Each called the other: Orphan! Would your teacher do this? One answered that he followed Shmuel; the other that he followed Rabbi Ḥiyya, who taught that the blessing over bread covers all foods and the blessing over wine covers all drinks.
why: Continuing the dispute between Rav and Shmuel over a fish from a meat bowl eaten with dairy, this story shows a student following Shmuel's lenient view in practice.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: One of the two Sages eating on either side of the ford.

people.name: Rav Ḥiyya bar Ashi
people.about: The other Sage; the two criticize each other's practice.

terms.meaning: A jab meaning a student with no teacher, implying the other's conduct shows he was never properly taught.
A Babylonian dip made with milk, so a dairy food.

note: Some kosher meat belonging to Rav Mari bar Raḥel was salted together with tereifa meat. He came to Rava, who ruled from the verse calling them the unclean: the definite article forbids not only their flesh but also their juices, gravy and spices. The Gemara asks why Rava did not cite Shmuel's rule that salted food acts like boiling food, and answers that Shmuel's rule might cover only blood, not juices and gravy.
why: Rav Naḥman has just ruled that fish salted together with birds absorb their blood; this case extends the question to kosher and non-kosher meat salted together, and Rava's answer forbids it.

people.name: Rav Mari bar Raḥel
people.about: His kosher meat was salted with non-kosher meat; he asks Rava what to do.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who rules the meat forbidden.

terms.meaning: An animal with a defect or wound that would have killed it within a year; its meat is forbidden even if slaughtered properly.
Kosher meat is salted to draw out its blood. Shmuel's rule treats salted food as passing on its flavor as if it were boiling hot.

note: In Rabbi Eliezer's locale they would cut down trees on Shabbat to make charcoal to forge iron for a circumcision, and in Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's locale they ate bird meat cooked in milk. Levi visited the house of Yosef the bird hunter and was served a peacock's head in milk, and said nothing. When he came before Rabbi, Rabbi asked why he had not excommunicated them. Levi said it was the town of Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira, and he thought Rabbi Yehuda might have taught them to follow Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, who said birds are excluded because they have no mother's milk.
why: The Gemara has just suggested that for Rabbi Yosei HaGelili bird meat in milk is not forbidden even by the Sages; the teaching about his town, and Levi's silence, bear that out.

people.name: Levi
people.about: A Sage served bird meat in milk who did not object.

people.name: Yosef the bird hunter
people.about: Levi's host, who served the peacock head in milk.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who asks Levi why he did not excommunicate them.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira
people.about: The Sage whose town this was; Levi thought he might have ruled leniently.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili
people.about: A Sage who held that bird meat is not included in the ban on meat and milk; his town ate it.

terms.meaning: A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna.
Place under a formal ban that cuts a person off from the community, a sanction for defying the Sages.

flag: Combines two items: a baraita on local customs in the towns of Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, and the separate story of Levi at Yosef the bird hunter's house.

note: Rav Avya the Elder put a hard question to Rabba bar Rav Huna: according to Rabbi Yishmael, does a sealed thigh bone of a carcass, which cannot make a person impure by touch, make him impure when he carries it? Instead of answering, Rabba bar Rav Huna said, "Look, a raven flies," to change the subject. His son Rava protested that this was the same Rav Avya his father always praised as a great man. Rabba bar Rav Huna explained that he was exhausted that day, quoting the Song of Songs, and the question needed careful reasoning he could not give on the spot.
why: The Gemara has just explained Rabbi Akiva's rule that what does not make impure by touch does not make impure by carrying; the unanswered question tests whether Rabbi Yishmael holds the same rule.

people.name: Rav Avya the Elder
people.about: A Sage of Pumbedita who asks the question; praised by Rabba bar Rav Huna as a great man

people.name: Rabba bar Rav Huna
people.about: The Sage who is asked and dodges the question because he is tired

people.name: Rava
people.about: Son of Rabba bar Rav Huna, who challenges his father's treatment of the guest

terms.meaning: The standard minimum amount, about the size of an olive, that a piece of a carcass must reach to transmit ritual impurity.
In Jewish law some impure things make a person ritually impure not only by touching them but also by lifting or carrying them, even without direct contact.

note: Rav Huna bar Torta told how he once went to the city of Va'ad and saw the locals placing a snake wrapped around a great lizard to breed them. After a time an arvad, a deadly biting snake, came out from between them. When he came before Rabbi Shimon the Righteous, Rabbi Shimon told him that God had said: they produced a creature I did not create in My world, so I will bring upon them a creature I did not create in My world.
why: The Gemara, returning to its survey of creatures and their kinds, follows the story by asking how a snake and a lizard with different gestation periods could breed at all; Rav answers that it was a miraculous calamity to punish the wicked.

people.name: Rav Huna bar Torta
people.about: The Sage who tells what he saw in Va'ad

people.name: Rabbi Shimon the Righteous
people.about: The Sage who explains the meaning of the event to Rav Huna bar Torta

people.name: The Holy One, Blessed be He
people.about: God, whose words Rabbi Shimon quotes, promising a creature-for-creature punishment

terms.meaning: A kind of snake that bites and kills people, here said to have come from crossbreeding a snake with a lizard.

note: Rabbi Tavla's host, a priest, was short of money. Rabbi Tavla advised him to go into partnership with Israelite butchers, who would take him in for free because a partnership with a priest exempts them from giving the priestly gifts. Rav Nahman nonetheless obligated the butcher to give the gifts and threatened to "remove Rabbi Tavla from your ear." Rabbi Tavla asked why; Rav Nahman cited a teaching that a priest who becomes a butcher is exempt for two or three weeks and then obligated. When Rabbi Tavla asked for at least those weeks, Rav Nahman said the exemption applies only to one who has not yet set up a shop, and this man already had.
why: The mishna exempts an animal owned jointly by an Israelite and a priest from the priestly gifts, and the Gemara has just said the gifts are claimed from the butcher; the story shows a Sage refusing to let that exemption be used as a business scheme.

people.name: Rabbi Tavla
people.about: A Sage whose host was a priest; he advises the partnership and later questions Rav Nahman's ruling

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: The judge who obligates the butcher to give the gifts despite the partnership

people.name: Rabbi Aha bar Hanina
people.about: A Sage who brought from the south the teaching Rav Nahman relies on

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
people.about: Sage who, with the elders of the south, said a priest-butcher is exempt only for his first weeks

terms.meaning: The foreleg, jaw and maw of a slaughtered animal, which the Torah says must be given to a priest (Deuteronomy 18:3).
A kohen, a descendant of Aaron, entitled to receive the priestly gifts.

note: Abaye, a priest, describes how his practice changed step by step. At first he would grab the priestly gifts, thinking this showed love for the commandment. When he learned the verse says the owner "shall give," he stopped grabbing and instead asked, "Give me." When he heard that the sons of Samuel sinned by asking for their portion, he stopped asking and only took what was offered. When he heard that the modest priests hold back while the gluttons take, he stopped taking at all, except on the eve of Yom Kippur, so that his standing as a priest would stay known.
why: Rav Yosef has just asked whether a priest who seizes his gifts honors or scorns the commandment, and Rava answered from the verse that he scorns it; Abaye's account shows that answer lived out, and the Gemara then asks why he did not prove his priesthood by giving the Priestly Benediction.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage who was a priest, telling how he came to stop taking the priestly gifts

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: Sage quoted in a teaching that the sons of Samuel sinned by asking for their portion

people.name: sons of Samuel
people.about: Levites who, the teaching says, sinned by demanding their portion out loud

terms.meaning: A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core collection of Jewish law.
Loaves displayed in the Temple each week and then divided among the priests to eat.
The day before the Day of Atonement, when it is a commandment to eat, so many animals were slaughtered and gifts were plentiful.

note: Rava and Rav Safra visited the house of Mar Yohana, who served them a choice calf. Rava asked Mar Yohana's attendant, a priest who normally received the priestly gifts, to grant them the gifts because he wanted to eat tongue with mustard. The attendant did; Rava ate and Rav Safra did not. Afterwards a verse from Proverbs was read to Rav Safra in a dream as a rebuke. He asked Rav Yosef whether it was because he had gone against Rav Yosef's ruling; Rav Yosef said no: his ruling covered only a priest giving freely to a needy scholar, not an attendant pressured into giving to a host's guest who could afford his own meat.
why: Rav Yosef has just ruled that a priest may assign his gifts to a poor Torah scholar; this incident marks the limits of that ruling, and the Gemara goes on to say the dream's rebuke was really meant for Rava.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who asks for the priestly gifts and eats them

people.name: Rav Safra
people.about: Rava's companion, who does not eat and receives a rebuking verse in a dream

people.name: Mar Yohana
people.about: Their host, son of Rav Hana bar Adda (or, some say, of Rav Hana bar Bizna)

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: The Sage whose ruling is in question and who explains its limits to Rav Safra

terms.meaning: The foreleg, jaw (with the tongue) and maw of a slaughtered animal, which must be given to a priest.
A calf considered especially choice and tender, served to honored guests.

note: Rav Kahana said he had seen the pigeons named for King Herod standing in sixteen rows, each a mil wide, calling out "My master, my master." One of them did not say it. Another said to it, "Blind one, say 'My master, my master.'" It answered, "Blind one, say 'My master, my slave'" - since Herod was not a king but a slave. They took that pigeon and slaughtered it. Rav Ashi reported that Rabbi Hanina said of this "words"; the Gemara will not have him dismissing Rav Kahana's report and reads it as "through words" of witchcraft.
why: The mishna mentions domesticated pigeons, and the Gemara has just recorded that one reading of their name ties them to King Herod, who bred them; Rav Kahana's tale follows from that name.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: The Sage who says he saw the pigeons himself

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Sage who reports Rabbi Hanina's comment on the story

people.name: Rabbi Hanina
people.about: Sage whose one-word comment the Gemara interprets

terms.meaning: A measure of distance used in the Talmud, roughly a kilometer.
King of Judea; the text says one name for these pigeons comes from him, as he bred them, and the pigeon calls him a slave rather than a king.

note: A certain man clipped a mother bird's wing, sent her away, and then caught her again. Rav Yehuda had him flogged and told him: go let her wings grow back, and then send her away.
why: Rav Yehuda has just taught that the mother bird must be sent far enough that she cannot be caught at once; the Gemara then asks whose view he followed, since flogging and sending her away seem to belong to different opinions, and answers that the lashes were rabbinic ones for defiance.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: The Sage who flogs the man and orders him to send the bird away properly

terms.meaning: The Torah commandment (Deuteronomy 22:6-7) that one who finds a nest must send away the mother before taking the eggs or chicks.
Whipped as a court punishment for breaking a commandment.

note: A man came to Rava asking whether the teima, a kosher bird, falls under the commandment of sending away the mother. Rava wondered aloud whether the man did not know that every kosher bird does. Pressed, the man said his doubt was about a nest with only a single egg, and Rava told him the mishna already rules that even one egg or one chick requires sending away the mother. The man sent the bird away, and Rava then surrounded her with nets and caught her. The Gemara asks whether Rava should have feared people would suspect his motive, and answers that he caught her in an unusual way.
why: The Gemara is discussing how a mother bird is to be sent away and whether she may be caught again afterwards; this incident shows that once she is properly sent off, catching her later is allowed.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who answers the man's question and then catches the released bird

terms.meaning: The name of a kosher bird the man was unsure about.
The early collection of Jewish law that the Gemara discusses; Rava quotes its ruling about a single egg.
The Torah commandment that one who finds a nest must send away the mother before taking the eggs or chicks.

note: Levi bar Simon transferred to Rav Yehuda the produce of his dovecote, its chicks and eggs. Rav Yehuda came to Shmuel, who told him: go bang on the nest so the birds rise up, and acquire them. The Gemara asks why this was needed and answers that this was a new brood Levi bar Simon himself did not yet own; banging on the nest would make the mothers fly up so that Levi bar Simon acquired the young, and he could then transfer them to Rav Yehuda by the formal handing over of a cloth.
why: The Gemara has just ruled that a courtyard cannot acquire eggs for its owner while the mother sits on them; this case of dovecote pigeons applies that ruling.

people.name: Levi bar Simon
people.about: Owner of a dovecote who gave its produce to Rav Yehuda

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: The recipient, who asks Shmuel how to take possession

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The Sage who tells Rav Yehuda to bang on the nest

terms.meaning: A structure where pigeons nest.

terms.term: acquisition by means of a cloth
terms.meaning: A formal way of transferring ownership: one party hands the other a cloth, and with it the deal becomes binding.
A Jewish holiday on which, as on the Sabbath, much work is forbidden; the Gemara considers whether the question was about preparing birds to slaughter on it.

note: A father told his son to climb to the top of a building and bring him fledglings. The son climbed up, sent away the mother bird and took the young, and on the way back down he fell and died. Rabbi Ya'akov asks where this son's long life and well-being went, since the Torah promises them for both of these commandments, and concludes that "that your days may be long" refers to the world that is entirely long, and "that it may go well with you" to the world where all is good.
why: Rabbi Ya'akov has just taught that every reward the Torah states for a commandment is paid in the World-to-Come; this case is his proof, and the Gemara goes on to test it by asking whether it really happened and whether the son was being punished for sinful thoughts.

terms.meaning: One of the Ten Commandments; like sending away the mother bird, the Torah promises long days for keeping it.
The Torah commandment that one who finds a nest must send away the mother before taking the young, with a promise of well-being and long life.

terms.term: the world that is entirely long
terms.meaning: Rabbi Ya'akov's reading of the promised long life as referring to the World-to-Come, the life after this one.
